claim: PBN neurons send dense projection fibers to the PVT.
source: Here, we show that PBN neurons send dense projection fibers to the PVT and form direct excitatory synapses with PVT neurons.
evidence: Supported by anatomical tracing data showing projection fibers in the PVT (Figure 1B).

claim: PBN neurons form direct excitatory synapses with PVT neurons.
source: Here, we show that PBN neurons send dense projection fibers to the PVT and form direct excitatory synapses with PVT neurons.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing monosynaptic EPSCs (Figure 1H-L).

claim: Activation of the PBN-PVT pathway induces robust behaviors associated with negative affective states.
source: Activation of the PBN-PVT pathway induces robust behaviors associated with negative affective states without affecting nociceptive behaviors.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic and pharmacogenetic activation experiments showing anxiety-like and aversion-like behaviors (Figures 2, 3).

claim: Activation of the PBN-PVT pathway does not affect nociceptive behaviors.
source: Activation of the PBN-PVT pathway induces robust behaviors associated with negative affective states without affecting nociceptive behaviors.
evidence: Supported by von Frey, Hargreaves, and formalin tests showing no changes in nociceptive thresholds (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C-F).

claim: Inhibition of the PBN-PVT pathway reduces aversion-like behaviors.
source: Inhibition of the PBN-PVT pathway reduces aversion-like and fear-like behaviors.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic inhibition experiments showing reduced aversion to 2-MT (Figure 4D-I).

claim: Inhibition of the PBN-PVT pathway reduces fear-like behaviors.
source: Inhibition of the PBN-PVT pathway reduces aversion-like and fear-like behaviors.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic inhibition experiments showing reduced footshock-induced freezing (Figure 4J-K).

claim: PVT neurons innervated by the PBN are activated by aversive stimulation.
source: Furthermore, the PVT neurons innervated by the PBN are activated by aversive stimulation, and activation of PBN-PVT projections enhances the neuronal activity of PVT neurons in response to the aversive stimulus.
evidence: Supported by Fos staining showing increased Fos expression in PVTPBN neurons after footshock and 2-MT exposure (Figure 5E-H).

claim: Activation of PBN-PVT projections enhances the neuronal activity of PVT neurons in response to aversive stimulus.
source: Furthermore, the PVT neurons innervated by the PBN are activated by aversive stimulation, and activation of PBN-PVT projections enhances the neuronal activity of PVT neurons in response to the aversive stimulus.
evidence: Supported by optoelectrode recordings showing increased firing rates during footshock with laser stimulation (Figure 6H-I).

claim: Activation of PVT neurons that received PBN-PVT projections induces anxiety-like behaviors.
source: Consistently, activation of PVT neurons that received PBN-PVT projections induces anxiety-like behaviors.
evidence: Supported by pharmacogenetic activation experiments showing reduced center time in OFT and reduced time in open quadrants in EZM (Figure 7F-I).

claim: PBN-PVT projections modulate negative affective states in mice.
source: Thus, our study indicates that PBN-PVT projections modulate negative affective states in mice.
evidence: Supported by multiple behavioral experiments showing effects on anxiety, aversion, and fear-like behaviors.

claim: The PBN plays a critical role in encoding danger signals and promoting affective behavior states to limit harm in response to potential threats.
source: It is worth noting that the parabrachial nucleus (PBN) in the brainstem plays a critical role in encoding danger signals and promoting affective behavior states to limit harm in response to potential threats (Campos et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Campos et al., 2018).

claim: The PBN receives the majority of the ascending inputs from the spinal cord.
source: The PBN receives the majority of the ascending inputs from the spinal cord (Todd, 2010), and PBN neurons respond robustly to nociception, food neophobia, hypercapnia, and threat to maintain homeostasis in stressful circumstances (Campos et al., 2018; Kaur et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Todd, 2010).

claim: PBN neurons respond robustly to nociception, food neophobia, hypercapnia, and threat to maintain homeostasis in stressful circumstances.
source: The PBN receives the majority of the ascending inputs from the spinal cord (Todd, 2010), and PBN neurons respond robustly to nociception, food neophobia, hypercapnia, and threat to maintain homeostasis in stressful circumstances (Campos et al., 2018; Kaur et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Campos et al., 2018; Kaur et al., 2013).

claim: Optogenetic activation of PBN projection fibers evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) in 34 of 52 PVT neurons.
source: We found that optogenetic activation of PBN projection fibers evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) in 34 of 52 PVT neurons.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing EPSCs in response to laser stimulation.

claim: The medial PVT showed 72.0% connectivity (18 of 25 cells).
source: The medial PVT (bregma: –0.94 to –1.82 mm; 18 of 25 cells, 72.0%) and posterior PVT (pPVT; bregma: –1.82 to –2.3 mm; 14 of 21 neurons, 66.7%) showed higher connectivity than the anterior PVT (bregma: –0.22 to –0.94 mm; 2 of 6 cells, 33.3%; Figure 1D–F).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings and shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: The posterior PVT showed 66.7% connectivity (14 of 21 neurons).
source: The medial PVT (bregma: –0.94 to –1.82 mm; 18 of 25 cells, 72.0%) and posterior PVT (pPVT; bregma: –1.82 to –2.3 mm; 14 of 21 neurons, 66.7%) showed higher connectivity than the anterior PVT (bregma: –0.22 to –0.94 mm; 2 of 6 cells, 33.3%; Figure 1D–F).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings and shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: The anterior PVT showed 33.3% connectivity (2 of 6 cells).
source: The medial PVT (bregma: –0.94 to –1.82 mm; 18 of 25 cells, 72.0%) and posterior PVT (pPVT; bregma: –1.82 to –2.3 mm; 14 of 21 neurons, 66.7%) showed higher connectivity than the anterior PVT (bregma: –0.22 to –0.94 mm; 2 of 6 cells, 33.3%; Figure 1D–F).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings and shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: The average amplitude of the light-evoked EPSCs was 103.4 ± 11.93 pA.
source: The average amplitude of the light-evoked EPSCs was 103.4 ± 11.93 pA (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The latency of EPSCs was short with small jitter, indicating monosynaptic connections between the PBN and PVT.
source: Moreover, the latency of EPSCs was short with small jitter (Figure 1I and J), indicating monosynaptic connections between the PBN and PVT.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 1I-J.

claim: The EPSCs were sensitive to the Na+ channel blocker tetrodotoxin (TTX, 1 μM).
source: Consistently, the EPSCs were sensitive to the Na+ channel blocker tetrodotoxin (TTX, 1 μM) and were rescued by the K+ channel blocker 4-aminopyridine (4-AP, 100 μM).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 1K-L.

claim: The EPSCs were rescued by the K+ channel blocker 4-aminopyridine (4-AP, 100 μM).
source: Consistently, the EPSCs were sensitive to the Na+ channel blocker tetrodotoxin (TTX, 1 μM) and were rescued by the K+ channel blocker 4-aminopyridine (4-AP, 100 μM).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 1K-L.

claim: The EPSCs were blocked by the AMPA receptor antagonist NBQX (10 μM).
source: The EPSCs were further blocked by the AMPA receptor antagonist NBQX (10 μM), confirming the monosynaptic glutamatergic innervation of PVT neurons by PBN neurons (Figure 1K and L).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 1K-L.

claim: Most monosynaptic connections between PBN and PVT are glutamatergic.
source: Thus, these results indicate that most monosynaptic connections between PBN and PVT are glutamatergic.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological and pharmacological experiments showing AMPA receptor-mediated EPSCs.

claim: Light-evoked inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) were observed in only 4 of 52 PVT neurons (less than 30 pA).
source: In addition, we also observed light-evoked inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) in only 4 of 52 PVT neurons (less than 30 pA).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: tdTomato+ neurons were bilaterally located in the lateral PBN (55 ± 6 neurons, n = 4 mice).
source: We found that tdTomato+ neurons were bilaterally located in the lateral PBN (55 ± 6 neurons, n = 4 mice) and rarely in the medial PBN (8 ± 1 neurons; Figure 1O–Q).
evidence: Supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 1O-Q.

claim: tdTomato+ neurons were rarely found in the medial PBN (8 ± 1 neurons).
source: We found that tdTomato+ neurons were bilaterally located in the lateral PBN (55 ± 6 neurons, n = 4 mice) and rarely in the medial PBN (8 ± 1 neurons; Figure 1O–Q).
evidence: Supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 1O-Q.

claim: Most PVT inputs originate in the lateral aspect of the PBN.
source: These results indicate that most PVT inputs originate in the lateral aspect of the PBN.
evidence: Supported by retrograde tracing showing more neurons in lateral PBN than medial PBN.

claim: Approximately 94.4% of tdTomato+ neurons expressed Slc17a6 mRNA (Vglut2+).
source: We then performed tdTomato staining and in situ hybridization with Slc17a6 (Vglut2) probe and found that approximately 94.4% of tdTomato+ neurons expressed Slc17a6 mRNA (Vglut2+, Figure 1R–U).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1R-U.

claim: tdTomato+ neurons were only partially co-labeled with Tacr1 mRNA (38.0%).
source: We found that tdTomato+ neurons were only partially co-labeled with Tacr1 mRNA (38.0%), Tac1 mRNA (6.4%), or Pdyn mRNA (23.0%) and not with CGRP protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: tdTomato+ neurons were only partially co-labeled with Tac1 mRNA (6.4%).
source: We found that tdTomato+ neurons were only partially co-labeled with Tacr1 mRNA (38.0%), Tac1 mRNA (6.4%), or Pdyn mRNA (23.0%) and not with CGRP protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: tdTomato+ neurons were only partially co-labeled with Pdyn mRNA (23.0%).
source: We found that tdTomato+ neurons were only partially co-labeled with Tacr1 mRNA (38.0%), Tac1 mRNA (6.4%), or Pdyn mRNA (23.0%) and not with CGRP protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: tdTomato+ neurons were not co-labeled with CGRP protein.
source: We found that tdTomato+ neurons were only partially co-labeled with Tacr1 mRNA (38.0%), Tac1 mRNA (6.4%), or Pdyn mRNA (23.0%) and not with CGRP protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The majority of PBN-PVT neurons are glutamatergic neurons.
source: These results indicate that the majority of PBN-PVT neurons are glutamatergic neurons, and most of these neurons are not labeled by Tacr1, Tac1, Pdyn, or CGRP.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization showing 94.4% Vglut2 expression.

claim: Most PBN-PVT neurons are not labeled by Tacr1, Tac1, Pdyn, or CGRP.
source: These results indicate that the majority of PBN-PVT neurons are glutamatergic neurons, and most of these neurons are not labeled by Tacr1, Tac1, Pdyn, or CGRP.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry showing low co-labeling percentages.

claim: The density of EGFP+ fibers was higher in the middle and pPVT.
source: It is worth noting that the density of EGFP+ fibers was higher in the middle and pPVT (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–H), considering the notion that the pPVT is particularly sensitive to aversion (Gao et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E-H and citation to previous literature (Gao et al., 2020).

claim: Collateral projections from PBN-PVT neurons were found in the BNST, LH, PVN, and PAG but not in the CeA or VMH.
source: We also found collateral projections from PBN-PVT neurons in the BNST, lateral hypothalamus (LH), paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVN), and PAG but not in the CeA or VMH (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Optogenetic activation of PBN-PVT projections elicited instant running behavior along the chamber wall with a significantly increased velocity.
source: Optogenetic activation (473 nm, 20 Hz, 5 mW, 5 ms) of the efferents from the PBN to the PVT elicited instant running behavior along the chamber wall with a significantly increased velocity (Figure 2F–H, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2F-H.

claim: Activation of PBN-PVT projections reduced the center time compared with that of the control mice.
source: The activation of PBN-PVT projections also reduced the center time compared with that of the control mice (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The velocity returned to normal once the laser was off, but the time spent in the center was still lower than that of the control group during the 5 min after stimulation.
source: It is worth noting that the velocity returned to normal once the laser was off, but the time spent in the center was still lower than that of the control group during the 5 min after stimulation.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from OFT experiments.

claim: Anxiety could last for at least several minutes after acute activation of PBN-PVT projections.
source: These results indicate that anxiety could last for at least several minutes after acute activation of PBN-PVT projections.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that center time remained low after laser was turned off.

claim: The immobility time of the ChR2 mice during the laser on period was increased.
source: Although the speed increased during the laser on period, the immobility time of the ChR2 mice during the laser on period was also increased (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The distance during the laser on period and the total distance in 15 min were not changed.
source: Therefore, the distance during the laser on period and the total distance in 15 min were not changed (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Optogenetic activation of PBN-PVT projections could induce brief and robust running, jumping behaviors, and persistent anxiety-like behaviors.
source: This detailed analysis indicates that optogenetic activation of PBN-PVT projections could induce brief and robust running, jumping behaviors, and persistent anxiety-like behaviors, such as less time spent in the center.
evidence: Supported by detailed behavioral analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-G.

claim: The activation of PBN-PVT projections reduced the time spent in the laser-paired chamber.
source: We found that the activation of PBN-PVT projections reduced the time spent in the laser-paired chamber, and the aversion disappeared when the laser was off (Figure 2K–M, Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: Supported by RTPA test data shown in Figure 2K-M.

claim: The aversion disappeared when the laser was off.
source: We found that the activation of PBN-PVT projections reduced the time spent in the laser-paired chamber, and the aversion disappeared when the laser was off (Figure 2K–M, Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: Supported by RTPA test data shown in Figure 2K-M.

claim: Prolonged activation of PBN-PVT projections did not display aversion in the postconditioning test.
source: We found that prolonged activation of PBN-PVT projections did not display aversion in the postconditioning test (Figure 2—figure supplement 2I).
evidence: Supported by prolonged CPA test data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2I.

claim: Activation of the PBN-PVT projections induced significant freezing behavior during six CS-LS pairings.
source: Activation of the PBN-PVT projections induced significant freezing behavior during six CS-LS pairings (Figure 2O).
evidence: Supported by cue-dependent optogenetic conditioning test data shown in Figure 2O.

claim: The freezing behavior to the same context or to the auditory cue in a novel context disappeared on the second day.
source: However, the freezing behavior to the same context or to the auditory cue in a novel context disappeared on the second day (Figure 2P and Q).
evidence: Supported by contextual and cue test data shown in Figure 2P-Q.

claim: Optogenetic activation of PBN-PVT projections induces instant aversion and freezing but does not drive associative fear memory formation.
source: These results indicate that optogenetic activation of PBN-PVT projections induces instant aversion and freezing but does not drive associative fear memory formation.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing transient effects without memory formation.

claim: Pharmacogenetic activation of PBN-PVT neurons reduced the center time in the OFT.
source: Consistent with the optogenetic activation results, pharmacogenetic activation of PBN-PVT neurons reduced the center time, increased immobility time, and reduced the travel distance in the OFT (Figure 3E–I).
evidence: Supported by OFT data shown in Figure 3E-I.

claim: Pharmacogenetic activation of PBN-PVT neurons increased immobility time in the OFT.
source: Consistent with the optogenetic activation results, pharmacogenetic activation of PBN-PVT neurons reduced the center time, increased immobility time, and reduced the travel distance in the OFT (Figure 3E–I).
evidence: Supported by OFT data shown in Figure 3E-I.

claim: Pharmacogenetic activation of PBN-PVT neurons reduced the travel distance in the OFT.
source: Consistent with the optogenetic activation results, pharmacogenetic activation of PBN-PVT neurons reduced the center time, increased immobility time, and reduced the travel distance in the OFT (Figure 3E–I).
evidence: Supported by OFT data shown in Figure 3E-I.

claim: Activation of PBN-PVT neurons did not affect motor ability in the rotarod test.
source: We also found that activation of PBN-PVT neurons did not affect motor ability in the rotarod test (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: Supported by rotarod test data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Pharmacogenetic activation of PBN-PVT neurons decreased exploration time of open quadrants in the elevated zero maze (EZM).
source: In addition, pharmacogenetic activation of PBN-PVT neurons decreased exploration time of open quadrants in the elevated zero maze (EZM; Figure 3K and L), further suggesting that activation of PBN-PVT neurons induces anxiety-like behaviors.
evidence: Supported by EZM data shown in Figure 3K-L.

claim: Pharmacogenetic activation of PBN-PVT neurons induced more freezing behaviors.
source: We further evaluated freezing behaviors in the fear conditioning chamber and found that pharmacogenetic activation of PBN-PVT neurons induced more freezing behaviors (Figure 3M and N).
evidence: Supported by freezing behavior data shown in Figure 3M-N.

claim: Activation of PBN-PVT neurons did not affect the depressive-like behaviors evaluated by the tail suspension test (TST).
source: Although activation of PBN-PVT neurons induced significant anxiety-like behavior, it did not affect the depressive-like behaviors evaluated by the tail suspension test (TST; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) or the forced swimming test (FST; Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by TST data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Activation of PBN-PVT neurons did not affect the depressive-like behaviors evaluated by the forced swimming test (FST).
source: Although activation of PBN-PVT neurons induced significant anxiety-like behavior, it did not affect the depressive-like behaviors evaluated by the tail suspension test (TST; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) or the forced swimming test (FST; Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by FST data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The basal nociceptive thresholds were not affected after pharmacogenetic activation of PBN-PVT neurons.
source: By performing the von Frey test and Hargreaves test, we found that the basal nociceptive thresholds were not affected after pharmacogenetic activation of PBN-PVT neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by von Frey and Hargreaves test data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C-D.

claim: Activation of PBN-PVT neurons did not affect formalin-evoked licking behaviors.
source: We found that activation of PBN-PVT neurons did not affect formalin-evoked licking behaviors (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E and F).
evidence: Supported by formalin test data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E-F.

claim: Activating the PBN-PVT pathway induces anxiety-like and freezing behaviors but not nociceptive behaviors.
source: These results indicate that activating the PBN-PVT pathway induces anxiety-like and freezing behaviors but not nociceptive behaviors.
evidence: Supported by multiple behavioral tests showing effects on anxiety and freezing but not nociception.

claim: Inhibition of PBN-PVT projections reduced the aversion caused by 2-MT exposure.
source: We found that 589 nm laser-induced inhibition of PBN-PVT projections reduced the aversion caused by 2-MT exposure (Figure 4D–F) and increased the moving duration (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by 2-MT aversion test data shown in Figure 4D-G.

claim: Inhibition of PBN-PVT projections increased the moving duration during 2-MT exposure.
source: We found that 589 nm laser-induced inhibition of PBN-PVT projections reduced the aversion caused by 2-MT exposure (Figure 4D–F) and increased the moving duration (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by 2-MT aversion test data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Inhibition of PBN-PVT projections increased the time spent in the 2-MT zone in the OFT.
source: We also observed that inhibition of PBN-PVT projections increased the time spent in the 2-MT zone in the OFT (Figure 4H–I).
evidence: Supported by OFT data shown in Figure 4H-I.

claim: Constant inhibition of PBN-PVT projections reduced footshock-induced freezing behaviors.
source: We found that constant inhibition of PBN-PVT projections reduced footshock-induced freezing behaviors (Figure 4J and K).
evidence: Supported by footshock-induced freezing data shown in Figure 4J-K.

claim: Inhibition of PBN-PVT projections did not affect aversive memory acquisition or retrieval.
source: We further compared freezing levels in contextual and cue tests without or with laser and found that aversive memory retrieval was not affected either (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by fear conditioning test data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C-D.

claim: Inhibition of the PBN-PVT pathway reduces aversion-like behaviors and footshock-induced freezing behaviors without affecting aversive memory acquisition or retrieval.
source: Thus, these results indicate that inhibition of the PBN-PVT pathway reduces aversion-like behaviors and footshock-induced freezing behaviors without affecting aversive memory acquisition or retrieval.
evidence: Supported by multiple behavioral tests showing effects on aversion and freezing but not memory.

claim: Calcium signals of PVT neurons were increased after the footshock and air puff.
source: To further examine the activity of the PVT in response to aversive stimulation, we performed the in vivo fiber photometry and found that calcium signals of PVT neurons were increased after the footshock and air puff (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The percentage of Fos+tdTomato+ neurons/tdTomato+ neurons in the PVT was significantly increased in the mice treated with aversive stimuli compared with that of control mice.
source: The percentage of Fos+tdTomato+ neurons/tdTomato+ neurons in the PVT was significantly increased in the mice treated with aversive stimuli compared with that of control mice (Figure 5E–H), confirming that the PVTPBN neurons could be activated by aversive stimuli.
evidence: Supported by Fos staining data shown in Figure 5E-H.

claim: PVTPBN neurons could be activated by aversive stimuli.
source: The percentage of Fos+tdTomato+ neurons/tdTomato+ neurons in the PVT was significantly increased in the mice treated with aversive stimuli compared with that of control mice (Figure 5E–H), confirming that the PVTPBN neurons could be activated by aversive stimuli.
evidence: Supported by Fos staining data shown in Figure 5E-H.

claim: There was a broad overlap between optogenetic stimulation-activated neurons (expressing the Fos protein) and footshock-activated neurons (expressing the fos mRNA).
source: We found that there was a broad overlap between optogenetic stimulation-activated neurons (expressing the Fos protein) and footshock-activated neurons (expressing the fos mRNA) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: Supported by dual Fos staining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-E.

claim: Laser or footshock (without laser) increased firing rates in 22 or 28, respectively, of 40 neurons.
source: We found that laser or footshock (without laser) increased firing rates in 22 or 28, respectively, of 40 neurons (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: Supported by optoelectrode recording data shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: There was a broad overlap between laser-activated and footshock-activated neurons.
source: There was also a broad overlap between laser-activated and footshock-activated neurons (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by optoelectrode recording data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: PVTPBN neurons were activated by aversive stimulation.
source: This result was consistent with the dual Fos staining result, suggesting that PVTPBN neurons were activated by aversive stimulation.
evidence: Supported by optoelectrode and Fos staining data showing overlap between laser-activated and footshock-activated neurons.

claim: The median response latency of 22 laser-activated neurons was 10 ms.
source: The median response latency of 22 laser-activated neurons was 10 ms, suggesting that monosynaptic inputs from PBN could increase the PVT activity.
evidence: Supported by optoelectrode recording data analyzing response latency.

claim: Monosynaptic inputs from PBN could increase the PVT activity.
source: The median response latency of 22 laser-activated neurons was 10 ms, suggesting that monosynaptic inputs from PBN could increase the PVT activity.
evidence: Inferred from the short response latency of laser-activated neurons.

claim: The footshock stimulus laser-activated 30 of 40 neurons.
source: We found that the footshock stimulus laser-activated 30 of 40 neurons (Figure 6H) and increased the overall firing rates of 40 neurons compared with the footshock without laser result (Figure 6I).
evidence: Supported by optoelectrode recording data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Footshock with laser increased the overall firing rates of 40 neurons compared with the footshock without laser result.
source: We found that the footshock stimulus laser-activated 30 of 40 neurons (Figure 6H) and increased the overall firing rates of 40 neurons compared with the footshock without laser result (Figure 6I).
evidence: Supported by optoelectrode recording data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Activation of PBN-PVT projections could enhance PVT neuronal responses to aversive stimulation.
source: These results indicate that activation of PBN-PVT projections could enhance PVT neuronal responses to aversive stimulation.
evidence: Supported by optoelectrode recording data showing increased firing rates during footshock with laser.

claim: The majority of the PVTPBN neurons could be activated by CNO in the hM3Dq-expressing mice but not the control mice.
source: The majority of the PVTPBN neurons could be activated by CNO in the hM3Dq-expressing mice but not the control mice, as demonstrated by the Fos staining (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: Supported by Fos staining data shown in Figure 7B-D.

claim: Pharmacogenetic activation of PVTPBN neurons reduced the center time in the OFT.
source: We found that pharmacogenetic activation of PVTPBN neurons reduced the center time (Figure 7E and F).
evidence: Supported by OFT data shown in Figure 7E-F.

claim: The time spent in open quadrants was decreased after activation of PVTPBN neurons in the EZM.
source: Similarly, the time spent in open quadrants was decreased and overall immobility time was increased in the EZM after activation of PVTPBN neurons (Figure 7G–I).
evidence: Supported by EZM data shown in Figure 7G-I.

claim: Overall immobility time was increased in the EZM after activation of PVTPBN neurons.
source: Similarly, the time spent in open quadrants was decreased and overall immobility time was increased in the EZM after activation of PVTPBN neurons (Figure 7G–I).
evidence: Supported by EZM data shown in Figure 7G-I.

claim: No obvious nociception-related behaviors were observed after activation of PVTPBN neurons.
source: We did not observe obvious nociception-related behaviors, such as forelimb wiping, hindlimb flinching, licking, or biting, after activation of PVTPBN neurons.
evidence: Based on behavioral observations during pharmacogenetic activation experiments.

claim: Pharmacogenetic activation of PVTPBN neurons induces anxiety-like behaviors.
source: These results indicate that pharmacogenetic activation of PVTPBN neurons induces anxiety-like behaviors.
evidence: Supported by OFT and EZM data showing reduced center time and reduced time in open quadrants.

claim: PVTPBN neurons sent projections to several brain areas, in particular the NAc, BNST, and CeA.
source: We found that PVTPBN neurons sent projections to several brain areas, in particular the NAc, BNST, and CeA (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–H), which was similar to early tracing research on PVT efferent projections (Li and Kirouac, 2008).
evidence: Supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B-H and citation to previous literature (Li and Kirouac, 2008).

claim: The PBN-CeA pathway was sufficient to drive behaviors associated with negative affective states.
source: Previous studies have reported that activation of the PBN-CeA pathway was sufficient to drive behaviors associated with negative affective states (Bowen et al., 2020; Cai et al., 2018; Han et al., 2015), enable associative learning, and generate aversive memory (Chiang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Bowen et al., 2020; Cai et al., 2018; Han et al., 2015; Chiang et al., 2020).

claim: The PBN-CeA pathway enables associative learning and generates aversive memory.
source: Previous studies have reported that activation of the PBN-CeA pathway was sufficient to drive behaviors associated with negative affective states (Bowen et al., 2020; Cai et al., 2018; Han et al., 2015), enable associative learning, and generate aversive memory (Chiang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Chiang et al., 2020).

claim: Activation of PBN-PVT projections induced only transient aversion-related behaviors.
source: Distinct from PBN-CeA projections, we found that activation of PBN-PVT projections induced only transient aversion-related behaviors, and inhibition of PBN-PVT projections did not affect fear memory acquisition or retrieval.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing transient effects in RTPA and no effects on fear conditioning.

claim: Inhibition of PBN-PVT projections did not affect fear memory acquisition or retrieval.
source: Distinct from PBN-CeA projections, we found that activation of PBN-PVT projections induced only transient aversion-related behaviors, and inhibition of PBN-PVT projections did not affect fear memory acquisition or retrieval.
evidence: Supported by fear conditioning test data showing no effects on memory.

claim: Only a few fluoro-gold (FG)/tetramethylrhodamine-dextran (TMR) double-labeled neurons were sparsely distributed in the PBN of mice injected with FG into the PVT and TMR into the CeA.
